claim_checks.section: ## 1. Context: one problem with two halves
claim_checks.claim: - Every registered claim is optional in RFC 7519 itself ✅[^1]
claim_checks.page_says: None of the claims defined below are intended to be mandatory to use or implement in all cases
claim_checks.note: RFC 7519 4.1 plus 'Use of this claim is OPTIONAL.' on each registered claim.

claim_checks.section: ## 1. Context: one problem with two halves
claim_checks.claim: Short access-token lifetimes make revocation of access tokens matter less, which moves the risk to the long-lived **refresh token**: it carries the client's full grant and is not tied to one API, so a stolen, replayable refresh token lets an attacker mint new access tokens ✅[^3]
claim_checks.page_says: allow the authorization server to issue access tokens with a short lifetime and reduced scope, thus reducing the potential impact of access token leakage.
claim_checks.note: The refresh-token half (full scope, not tied to one resource, replay mints access tokens) is in RFC 9700 4.14. The leading clause is not: the page says short lifetimes reduce the impact of leakage, not that revocation matters less, and it never calls refresh tokens long-lived.

claim_checks.claim: | Access token | Client holds; RS receives on every call | No standard value; RFC 10017 recommends reducing it and renewing with refresh tokens. Minutes are common in practice | — | ✅[^2]; "minutes are common" ⚠️ unverified |
claim_checks.page_says: Reduce the lifetime of access tokens and rely on refresh tokens for access token renewal
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 9.1; the RFC gives no fixed value, only 'minutes to hours' as typical (5.2.2).

claim_checks.claim: | Refresh token | Client holds; only the AS receives it | Set by the AS. One vendor's rotation default: 30 days absolute, at most 1 year, and rotation does not extend it | Without one, the client re-runs the authorization flow, possibly silently with the AS session cookie | ✅[^15] ✅[^3] |
claim_checks.page_says: The default refresh token expiration period, when Refresh Token Rotation is enabled, is 30 days (2,592,000 seconds). You can configure up to 1 year
claim_checks.note: Auth0 also says 'The lifetime does not extend when tokens are rotated.' RFC 9700 4.14: without refresh tokens the client MAY use the authorization code grant and the AS may use cookies to smooth it.

claim_checks.claim: | BFF session cookie | Browser holds; BFF receives | Should match the refresh token's maximum lifetime; when the refresh token dies, the BFF should end the session | — | ✅[^2] |
claim_checks.page_says: it makes sense to configure the lifetime of the cookie-based session managed by the BFF to be equal to the maximum lifetime of the refresh token
claim_checks.note: Same paragraph: when the refresh token is no longer valid 'it also makes sense to invalidate the session'. Advisory wording matches the doc's lowercase 'should'.

claim_checks.claim: | DPoP proof | Client creates per request; AS or RS receives | Short; bound to method (`htm`), URL (`htu`), time (`iat`), access-token hash (`ath`) and optional server nonce | Without it, the token is a plain bearer token | ✅[^11] |
claim_checks.page_says: When the DPoP proof is used in conjunction with the presentation of an access token in protected resource access (see Section 7), the DPoP proof MUST also contain
claim_checks.note: The row says the proof is received by the AS or RS and is bound to ath with no condition; ath is required only when the proof accompanies an access token at a protected resource, not at the token endpoint. Dropped condition.

claim_checks.claim: | `__Host-` name prefix | Browser stores it only with `Secure`, no `Domain`, `Path=/` | — | ✅[^12]; lab: a `__Host-` cookie with `Domain=` and one without `Secure` were both dropped ✅[^25] |
claim_checks.page_says: not found (local lab artifact, no saved text)
claim_checks.note: Cites only the local cookie lab.

claim_checks.claim: | `__Host-Http-` name prefix | `__Host-` rules plus `HttpOnly`, so only a `Set-Cookie` header can set it | — | ✅[^12]; lab: a `__Host-Http-` cookie without `HttpOnly` was dropped ✅[^25] |
claim_checks.page_says: must have the HttpOnly attribute set to prove that they were set via the Set-Cookie header. In addition, they also have the same restrictions as __Host--prefixed cookies.
claim_checks.note: MDN cookie prefixes, __Host-Http- entry.

claim_checks.claim: | Revoke on security events | Ends refresh tokens on password change or logout at the AS | Optional ("may") | ✅[^3] |
claim_checks.page_says: Authorization servers MAY revoke refresh tokens automatically in case of a security event, such as:
claim_checks.note: Listed events: password change, logout at the authorization server.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. Threat model: what injected JavaScript can do
claim_checks.claim: No practical client-side defence; DPoP does not help either ✅[^2]
claim_checks.page_says: There are no practical security mechanisms for frontend applications that counter this attack scenario. ... Advanced security mechanism, such as DPoP [RFC9449], are equally ineffective

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Where the browser can keep a token
claim_checks.claim: | `sessionStorage` | Yes | No | Yes / no, per tab | Slightly smaller exposure (§8.5) | ✅[^2] ✅[^13] |
claim_checks.page_says: sessionStorage is not shared between multiple tabs open to pages on the same origin, which slightly reduces the exposure of the tokens in sessionStorage.
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 8.5 also ties its lifetime to the tab; OWASP HTML5: available only to that window/tab until it is closed.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Where the browser can keep a token
claim_checks.claim: | Web Worker or Service Worker memory | Not directly; the page must ask the worker | No | Worker-dependent | Isolated, but the attacker can still run its own flow; a service worker must not keep tokens in storage shared with the page (§8.2, §8.3) | ✅[^2] |
claim_checks.page_says: the Service Worker MUST NOT store tokens in any persistent storage API that is shared with the main window.
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 8.2 (when isolating tokens); 8.2/8.3 also say a worker does not stop the attacker obtaining new tokens.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Where the browser can keep a token
claim_checks.claim: The lab page ran this from its own JavaScript, the position an XSS payload runs in, in Chromium 152 (the Claude desktop app's browser) and Chrome 158 headless ✅[^25]
claim_checks.page_says: not found (local lab artifact, no saved text)
claim_checks.note: Cites only the local cookie lab.

claim_checks.claim: Refresh-token theft and new-token acquisition are mitigated; access tokens are exposed to theft by injected code; CSRF defences are needed on the endpoint that hands out access tokens; RFC 10017 says to use it only when a full BFF is not viable ✅[^2]
claim_checks.page_says: Only when the use cases or system requirements would prevent the use of a proxying BFF should the token-mediating backend be considered over a full BFF.
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 6.2.4.1-6.2.4.4 and 6.2.3.3 cover the mitigated scenarios, access-token exposure and CSRF on the token endpoints.

claim_checks.claim: Its refresh tokens must be rotated or sender-constrained ✅[^3]
claim_checks.page_says: Refresh tokens for public clients MUST be sender-constrained or use refresh token rotation as described in Section 4.14.

claim_checks.claim: The browser attaches the `HttpOnly` cookie, as the lab showed for same-origin `fetch` ✅[^25]
claim_checks.page_says: not found (local lab artifact, no saved text)
claim_checks.note: Cites only the local cookie lab.

claim_checks.claim: `Path=/auth/refresh` reduces where the cookie travels but is not a security boundary ✅[^12]
claim_checks.page_says: It is not intended as a security measure, and does not protect against unauthorized reading of the cookie from a different path.
claim_checks.note: MDN note on the Path attribute.

claim_checks.claim: | Single-execution theft | mitigated ✅[^2] | access token exposed ✅[^2] | exposed ✅[^2] | access token exposed ⚠️ unverified |
claim_checks.page_says: The other attack scenarios, listed below, are effectively mitigated by the BFF application architecture:
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 6.1.4.2; the list starts with Single-Execution Token Theft (5.1.1).

claim_checks.claim: access token exposed ✅[^2]
claim_checks.page_says: the access token becomes vulnerable to token theft by malicious browser-based code.
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 6.2.4.1 lists Persistent Token Theft for access tokens as relevant.

claim_checks.claim: | 6.7 | Token Status List | One token | The list's `ttl` or HTTP cache time | Fetch and cache one compressed list per many tokens | Unique lists defeat privacy | ✅[^8] |
claim_checks.page_says: If caching-related HTTP headers are present in the HTTP response, Relying Parties MUST prioritize the exp and ttl claims within the Status List Token over the HTTP headers
claim_checks.note: The other cells entail (one list for many tokens, unique lists defeat herd privacy). The delay cell's alternative 'HTTP cache time' is not what the draft gives: caching is conveyed by ttl and exp (11.5, 13.7), which MUST override HTTP headers; the changelog says HTTP caching was removed in favour of ttl.

claim_checks.claim: Short access tokens limit how long a revoked grant can still be used ✅[^6]
claim_checks.page_says: issue short-lived access tokens ... This allows the authorization server to impose a limit on the time revoked when access tokens are in use.
claim_checks.note: RFC 7009 section 3.

claim_checks.claim: - `EXAT` sets an absolute Unix expiry in seconds ✅[^17]; an `EXPIREAT` time already in the past deletes the key at once ✅[^16], so revoking an already-expired token stores nothing.
claim_checks.page_says: calling EXPIRE/PEXPIRE with a non-positive timeout or EXPIREAT/PEXPIREAT with a time in the past will result in the key being deleted rather than expired
claim_checks.note: Claim stops at the mark; the following 'so revoking an already-expired token stores nothing' (about SET ... EXAT) is outside it.

claim_checks.claim: Lab output ✅[^24]:
claim_checks.page_says: not found (local lab artifact, no saved text)
claim_checks.note: Cites only the local revocation lab.

claim_checks.claim: Node.js's `Buffer` decoder for `base64url` accepts the regular base64 alphabet by design ✅[^20]
claim_checks.page_says: When creating a Buffer from a string, this encoding will also correctly accept regular base64-encoded strings.
claim_checks.note: Node.js Buffer docs, 'base64url' encoding.

claim_checks.claim: The OWASP cheat sheet itself used to hash the token for its denylist and switched to `jti`-based keys in June 2026 ✅[^5]
claim_checks.page_says: The OWASP JWT Cheat Sheet used to recommend a revocation list based on hashed JWTs / Replaced the SHA-256 digest-based denylist with one keyed on the jti (JWT ID) claim
claim_checks.note: PR 2242 shows 'Merged' on Jun 22, 2026. Grounded, but both sources are rank 6 in a role-3 section (KB-15 breach, logged separately).

claim_checks.claim: NumericDate allows fractions ✅[^1]
claim_checks.page_says: other than that non-integer values can be represented.
claim_checks.note: RFC 7519 NumericDate definition.

claim_checks.claim: For self-contained access tokens, stopping them at the RS needs some non-standard link between AS and RS, which is why short lifetimes are paired with it ✅[^6]
claim_checks.page_says: some (currently non-standardized) backend interaction between the authorization server and the resource server may be used when immediate access token revocation is desired.
claim_checks.note: Same paragraph offers short-lived access tokens as the alternative design.

claim_checks.claim: Refresh-token revocation is required; access-token revocation is recommended; revoking a refresh token should also invalidate access tokens of the same grant when the AS supports that ✅[^6]
claim_checks.page_says: Implementations MUST support the revocation of refresh tokens and SHOULD support the revocation of access tokens ... the authorization server SHOULD also invalidate all access tokens
claim_checks.note: The SHOULD is conditioned on the AS supporting access-token revocation, as the claim says.

claim_checks.claim: - D3: rotation detects nothing when the legitimate client never presents its last token again, which is why RFC 10017 says rotation alone does not stop persistent theft ✅[^2]
claim_checks.page_says: Since the application will not use the latest refresh token, there will be no detectable refresh token reuse, giving the attacker full control over the stolen refresh token.
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 5.1.2: 'Refresh token rotation is not sufficient to prevent abuse of a refresh token.'

claim_checks.claim: Each request carries a DPoP proof: a JWT with header `typ: dpop+jwt` and the public key, and claims `jti`, `htm` (method), `htu` (URL), `iat`, plus `ath` (hash of the access token) and the server's `nonce` when required ✅[^11]
claim_checks.page_says: The payload of a DPoP proof MUST contain at least the following claims:
claim_checks.note: RFC 9449 4.2 lists typ dpop+jwt, alg, jwk in the header; jti, htm, htu, iat in the payload; ath with an access token; nonce when the server supplied DPoP-Nonce.

claim_checks.claim: The OP posts `logout_token=<JWT>` to each client's registered `backchannel_logout_uri`; the client validates it (signature, `iss`, `aud`, `iat`, `exp`, `events` containing `http://schemas.openid.net/event/backchannel-logout`, `sub` or `sid`, no `nonce`), ends the matching sessions, and answers `200` (or `204`); refresh tokens without `offline_access` should be revoked, those with it normally kept ✅[^9]
claim_checks.page_says: Refresh tokens issued without the offline_access property to a session being logged out SHOULD be revoked. Refresh tokens issued with the offline_access property normally SHOULD NOT be revoked.
claim_checks.note: Sections 2.5-2.8 cover the logout_token POST to the registered URI, the validation list (including no nonce), clearing session state, and 200 with 204 tolerated.

claim_checks.claim: Against malware that copies cookies, Chrome's DBSC has the browser create a per-session key pair in hardware (TPM, Trusted Platform Module, on Windows; Secure Enclave on macOS) and prove possession before the server issues new short-lived cookies; it reached public availability on Windows in Chrome 146, announced 2026-04-09 ✅[^19]
claim_checks.page_says: The issuance of new short-lived session cookies is contingent upon Chrome proving possession of the corresponding private key to the server.
claim_checks.note: Same post: TPM on Windows and Secure Enclave on macOS, a distinct key per session, 'entering public availability for Windows users on Chrome 146', dated Apr 09, 2026.

claim_checks.claim: | BFF deletes a session | Next call is unauthenticated | Stops using that session's tokens | Unaware unless told (revoke or logout) | Unaware; the BFF simply stops calling | Proxying through the old cookie stops | ✅[^2] |
claim_checks.page_says: Doing so ensures a great level of control over active sessions, along with the possibility to revoke any session at will.
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 supports ending access by deleting a server-side session; the AS and RS cells ('unaware unless told', 'the BFF simply stops calling') are not in the page.

claim_checks.claim: | User logs out at the AS | — | Gets a logout token if registered; ends sessions, revokes refresh tokens without `offline_access` | Sends back-channel logout | Self-contained access tokens remain valid until `exp` unless checked | — | ✅[^9] ✅[^6] |
claim_checks.page_says: Refresh tokens issued without the offline_access property to a session being logged out SHOULD be revoked.
claim_checks.note: The row states as plain behaviour that the client revokes these refresh tokens; the spec says SHOULD. The RS cell is supported by RFC 7009 sections 3 and 5.

claim_checks.claim: | Password change | — | — | May revoke refresh tokens | Access tokens remain valid until `exp` unless checked | Loses refresh, keeps access briefly | ✅[^3] ✅[^6] |
claim_checks.page_says: Authorization servers MAY revoke refresh tokens automatically in case of a security event, such as:
claim_checks.note: The AS cell keeps the MAY, but the attacker cell 'Loses refresh, keeps access briefly' states the loss as certain; it holds only if the AS chose to revoke.

claim_checks.section: ## 8. Worked example: one full pass through a BFF
claim_checks.claim: Revoked at the AS (RFC 7009) ✅[^6]
claim_checks.page_says: The invalidation takes place immediately, and the token cannot be used again after the revocation.

claim_checks.section: ## 8. Worked example: one full pass through a BFF
claim_checks.claim: | Sessions at other apps | When each back-channel POST arrives | Logout token ✅[^9] |
claim_checks.page_says: the RP locates the session(s) identified by the iss and sub Claims and/or the sid Claim. The RP then clears any state associated with the identified session(s).
claim_checks.note: Back-Channel Logout 2.7.

claim_checks.claim: | 4 | XSS calls APIs through the BFF | Works while the page is open | Fix the XSS; CSP (Content Security Policy) as a second layer | ✅[^2] ✅[^11] |
claim_checks.page_says: Besides secure coding practices, Content Security Policy [W3C.CSP] can be used as a second layer of defense against XSS.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9449 11.4; RFC 10017 6.1.4.1 says nothing prevents proxying apart from stopping the malicious code.

claim_checks.claim: | 4 | XSS calls APIs through the BFF | Works while the page is open | Fix the XSS; CSP (Content Security Policy) as a second layer | ✅[^2] ✅[^11] |
claim_checks.page_says: nothing will be able to prevent such attacks apart from stopping the execution of malicious code in the first place.
claim_checks.note: RFC 10017 6.1.4.1, which also names CSP as defense in depth.

claim_checks.claim: | 9 | Logout and re-login in the same second with an `iat` cut-off | Stolen token survives, or re-login fails | Version counter | ✅[^24] |
claim_checks.page_says: not found (local lab artifact, no saved text)
claim_checks.note: Cites only the local revocation lab.

claim_checks.claim: | 11 | Introspection answer cached | Revoked token accepted until the cache entry ends | Short cache; never past `exp` | ✅[^7] |
claim_checks.page_says: This creates a window during which a revoked token could be used at the protected resource. ... the response MUST NOT be cached beyond the time indicated therein.
claim_checks.note: RFC 7662 section 4; 'a less aggressive cache with a short timeout' supports the short-cache mitigation.

claim_checks.claim: | 12 | Refresh token revoked, access token self-contained | Access token works until `exp` | Short lifetime or RS-side check | ✅[^6] |
claim_checks.page_says: If the authorization server does not support access token revocation, access tokens will not be immediately invalidated when the corresponding refresh token is revoked.
claim_checks.note: RFC 7009 sections 3 and 5.

claim_checks.claim: **Short access tokens** plus a revocation check where "log out" must be immediate: a per-user version counter for "everywhere", (`iss`, `jti`) or `sid` for one token or session, with entries expiring at the token's `exp` ✅[^4]
claim_checks.page_says: A JWT deny list can typically be implemented based on the jti and iss claims: ... deny_list.insert((jti, iss), exp)
claim_checks.note: OWASP also gives short expiration, a 'deny list of revoked sessions/tokens' and 'other claims might be more suitable' (covers sid). The per-user version counter rests only on the local lab [^24], which cannot be checked.

claim_checks.claim: 6. **Tell the other apps:** back-channel logout or CAEP events, so a logout at the AS reaches every client ✅[^9] ✅[^10].
claim_checks.page_says: Relying Parties supporting back-channel-based logout register a back-channel logout URI with the OP as part of their client registration.
claim_checks.note: 'reaches every client' widens scope: back-channel logout reaches only RPs that registered a logout URI (and the OP does not retransmit except on suspected recoverable errors); CAEP runs between cooperating Transmitters and Receivers.

claim_checks.claim: In headless Chrome the IndexedDB step never completed, so that one result comes from Chromium 152 only ✅[^25]
claim_checks.page_says: not found (local lab artifact, no saved text)
claim_checks.note: Cites only the local cookie lab.

conflicts.topic: Reuse detection: RFC 9700 has the AS revoke the active refresh token; Auth0 revokes the whole token family
OWASP denylist key: PR 2242's title says jti+aud; the current cheat sheet keys on (jti, iss)

criteria_checks.criterion: LS-03 pass: Section 5 (role 5) must enforce HttpOnly; Secure cookies
criteria_checks.evidence: Role 5 = sections 4, 10, 11. Section 10 item 1 sets the session cookie as '__Host-Http-…; Secure; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Strict' ✅[^2]. Section 4 lists the backend-set HttpOnly cookie as the only storage injected script cannot read and marks JS-set cookies 'Not recommended'. The normative MUST (RFC 10017 6.1.3.2) is quoted in 5.1, which maps to role 2.

criteria_checks.criterion: LS-03 pass: Section 6 (role 6) must explain the stateless revocation trade-off
criteria_checks.evidence: Role 6 = sections 7 and 9. Section 7: a denylist or version check costs 'One lookup per request; must decide what to do if the store is down', and self-contained access tokens stay valid until exp unless checked. Section 9 rows 8 and 12: fail open vs fail closed; a self-contained token works until exp, fixed by a short lifetime or an RS-side check. The plain 'a denylist removes the statelessness' sentence sits outside role 6, in 5.5 (role 2) and 6.5 (role 3).

criteria_checks.criterion: Ground truth: localStorage is exposed to XSS; stateless JWTs cannot be revoked at once without a deny-list
criteria_checks.evidence: Section 4: localStorage 'Readable by injected script? Yes' ✅[^2], with a lab readout. 1.1: the copied token is ACCEPTED after logout ✅[^24]. Summary and 6.5: ending a token at once needs state.

criteria_checks.criterion: Conflict trap not stated as true in roles 1-5 ('store JWTs securely in localStorage and delete them client-side to log out')
criteria_checks.evidence: No role 1-5 text recommends localStorage or client-side deletion. 1.1 shows the opposite ('client deletes its copy; server keeps no state' -> token ACCEPTED).

No row in section 7 or 9 names localStorage or client-side deletion as a logout. Section 9 row 12 and the section 7 'User logs out at the AS' row only cover the second half (tokens live until exp). The refutation lives in roles 1, 4 and 5 (1.1, section 8's closing paragraph, section 4).

violations.section: ## 1. Context: one problem with two halves
violations.evidence: S2 (unsupported): The refresh-token half (full scope, not tied to one resource, replay mints access tokens) is in RFC 9700 4.14. The leading clause is not: the page says short lifetimes reduce the impact of leakage, not that revocation matters less, and it never calls refresh tokens long-lived.

S6 (overstates): The row says the proof is received by the AS or RS and is bound to ath with no condition; ath is required only when the proof accompanies an access token at a protected resource, not at the token endpoint. Dropped condition.

S20 (unsupported): The other cells entail (one list for many tokens, unique lists defeat herd privacy). The delay cell's alternative 'HTTP cache time' is not what the draft gives: caching is conveyed by ttl and exp (11.5, 13.7), which MUST override HTTP headers; the changelog says HTTP caching was removed in favour of ttl.
S33 (unsupported): RFC 10017 supports ending access by deleting a server-side session; the AS and RS cells ('unaware unless told', 'the BFF simply stops calling') are not in the page.
S34 (overstates): The row states as plain behaviour that the client revokes these refresh tokens; the spec says SHOULD. The RS cell is supported by RFC 7009 sections 3 and 5.
S35 (overstates): The AS cell keeps the MAY, but the attacker cell 'Loses refresh, keeps access briefly' states the loss as certain; it holds only if the AS chose to revoke.

S44 (overstates): 'reaches every client' widens scope: back-channel logout reaches only RPs that registered a logout URI (and the OP does not retransmit except on suspected recoverable errors); CAEP runs between cooperating Transmitters and Receivers.

The conflict-trap claim (keep JWTs in localStorage and log out by deleting them client-side) is refuted in role 1 (1.1 lab: copied token ACCEPTED after the client deleted its copy) and role 5 (section 4: localStorage readable by injected script), but no role-6 row names it. Role 6 only covers it in part: 9 row 12 and the 7 'User logs out at the AS' row say self-contained tokens live until exp.

The role-3 section also holds role-6 material: the malleability pitfall in 6.2, the same-second bug in 6.3 and benign-race failures in 6.10. The rank-6 citations sit in that material. The 6.0 catalogue is role-5 content.

patch_instructions.action: 6.2, line 306: drop ✅[^5] from 'Never key the denylist on the raw token or its hash'. Keep ✅[^4]: OWASP warns that raw-token or SHA-256 keys allow 'denylist bypass through JWT malleability' because of non-strict parsing and ECDSA malleability.

6.2, line 308: in role 3 keep only 'non-strict JWT parsing lets an altered string still verify ✅[^4]', plus the Node.js sentence ✅[^20] and the lab ✅[^24]. Move the 43-character / 2-unused-bit arithmetic and the padding and alphabet details, cited [^5] (rank 6), to a row in section 9.
6.2, line 309: replace with 'For ECDSA JWTs, the signature itself is malleable ✅[^4]' and keep the lab ES256 result ✅[^24]. Move the (r, n − s) formula and the EdDSA remark, cited [^5], to section 9.
6.2, line 318: move the PyJWT 2.13.0 / java-jwt 4.5.2 library results ✅[^5] to section 9 (role 6), labelled as a rank-6 report that was not re-tested.

6.2, line 318: move 'The OWASP cheat sheet itself used to hash the token ... switched to jti-based keys in June 2026 ✅[^5] ✅[^23]' to section 9, or drop it. Role 3 already states the current OWASP rule, (jti, iss) ✅[^4].
Item 5: drop ✅[^5]. Keep ✅[^4]: OWASP supports the algorithm allow-list ('Make sure that "alg":"none" is not accepted'), and its non-strict-parsing and raw-token warnings support the rest.

patch_instructions.section: ## 1. Context: one problem with two halves
patch_instructions.action: 1.2, S2: drop 'make revocation of access tokens matter less' and 'long-lived', or back them with the right source: RFC 7009 section 3 [^6] says short-lived access tokens let the AS 'impose a limit on the time revoked when access tokens are in use'. With [^3], keep only what RFC 9700 4.14 says: short lifetimes reduce the impact of access-token leakage, and refresh tokens carry the full grant and are not tied to one resource.
6.0 row 6.7, S20: change the delay cell to "The list's `ttl`, or until its `exp`". Draft 21 sections 11.5 and 13.7 [^8] say ttl and exp carry caching and MUST take priority over HTTP cache headers.
2.2 DPoP proof row, S6: write 'access-token hash (`ath`) when the proof accompanies an access token at the RS' (RFC 9449 4.2 [^11]).

Item 6, S44: change 'reaches every client' to 'reaches every client that registered a back-channel logout URI (or receives CAEP events), when delivery succeeds' (Back-Channel Logout 2.2 and 2.5 [^9]; CAEP [^10]).
Row 'BFF deletes a session', S33: mark the AS and RS cells ⚠️ unverified or drop them. RFC 10017 6.1.2.3 [^2] supports only 'the possibility to revoke any session at will'.
Row 'User logs out at the AS', S34: write 'should revoke refresh tokens without offline_access' (Back-Channel Logout 2.7 [^9], SHOULD).
Row 'Password change', S35: change the attacker cell to 'Loses refresh only if the AS revokes it (optional, "may"); keeps access until exp' (RFC 9700 4.14 [^3]; RFC 7009 section 3 [^6]).

Add a row: 'Tokens in localStorage; logout only deletes the client copy' | 'Any injected script could already have copied it, and a copied token is accepted until exp' | 'BFF with an HttpOnly session cookie; server-side revocation (denylist or version counter)'. Evidence: RFC 10017 8.5 [^2] ('localStorage does not protect against unauthorized access from malicious JavaScript') and the 1.1 lab [^24].

Structure: keep 6.1-6.13 to how each mechanism works. Move the malleability pitfall (6.2), the same-second bug (6.3) and the benign-race findings (6.10, D4-D5) into section 9 as failure rows, leaving one-line pointers.
